entry: Competitive situation in [[Game theory|game theory]] in which one participant's gain equals another's loss, so the net change in benefit is zero. Cutting a cake is a zero-sum game if all participants value each unit equally. In daily life, [[Poker|poker]], [[Chess|chess]] and [[Sport|sport]] are zero-sum, as are futures contracts and options in markets. Zero-sum games are also called strictly competitive games and are most often solved with the [[Minimax|minimax theorem]] or with [[Nash equilibrium|Nash equilibrium]]. In contrast, positive-sum games allow aggregate gains and losses to exceed zero; the [[Prisoner's dilemma|Prisoner's Dilemma]] is a classic non-zero-sum game.

Supreme deity of the Greek pantheon, a sky and thunder god who ruled as king of the gods on [[Mount Olympus|Mount Olympus]]. In most traditions he was the youngest child of Cronus and Rhea. He and his brothers [[Poseidon|Poseidon]] and Hades defeated their father's generation of gods, the [[Titans|Titans]], and divided the cosmos, with Zeus receiving the sky. He was married to his sister [[Hera|Hera]]. His many offspring included [[Athena|Athena]], [[Apollo|Apollo]], Artemis and [[Hermes|Hermes]], as well as the Muses. His symbols included the thunderbolt and the eagle. Worship was widespread across the Greek world, with major sanctuaries at Olympia, site of the ancient Olympic Games held in his honor, and at Dodona, where oracles were consulted through the rustling of sacred oak leaves. In ancient Rome he was identified with [[Jupiter|Jupiter]].

Chinese polymathic scientist and statesman of the Eastern [[Han dynasty|Han dynasty]]. He rose from a minor civil service post to become Chief Astronomer and a palace attendant at the imperial court. His uncompromising stance on historical and calendrical issues kept him from becoming Grand Historian. After a rivalry with palace [[Eunuch|eunuchs]] under Emperor Shun, he left the central court to administer Hejian Kingdom in present-day Hebei. He invented the world's first water-powered armillary sphere and the world's first seismoscope, which indicated the direction of an earthquake 500 km (310 mi) away. His star catalog recorded about 2,500 stars, and he improved earlier Chinese calculations of [[Pi|pi]]. He also described the Moon's sphericity and its illumination by reflected sunlight, and the nature of solar and lunar eclipses. His *fu* and *shi* poetry was renowned in his time, and some modern scholars have compared his astronomy with that of [[Ptolemy|Ptolemy]].

Chinese diplomat and explorer who served as an imperial envoy to the world beyond China under [[Emperor Wu of Han|Emperor Wu of Han]]. In 138 BC he set out with a group of ninety-nine members to seek an alliance against the Xiongnu, but he was captured and held for thirteen years. After escaping, he spent a year among the Yuezhi and in the adjacent [[Bactria|Bactrian]] territory, documenting their cultures, lifestyles and economy, before returning to China. His reports on [[Central Asia|Central Asia]] informed the Han court, and his missions opened the routes that became the [[Silk Road|Silk Road]], which marked the beginning of globalization between East and West. His accounts were compiled by [[Sima Qian|Sima Qian]]. Today Zhang is considered a Chinese national hero.

Coastal province of eastern China (pop., 2024: 66.7 million), with its capital at [[Hangzhou|Hangzhou]]. Hills cover about 70% of its area. The province has a longer coastline than any other mainland province and three thousand islands, the most in China. It takes its name from the Qiantang River, which runs through it. The area was controlled by the Kingdom of Yue during the Spring and Autumn period and was annexed by the [[Qin dynasty|Qin dynasty]] in 222 BC. Under the late [[Ming dynasty|Ming dynasty]] and the [[Qing dynasty|Qing dynasty]], its ports became important centers of international trade. Its economy stagnated under [[Mao Zedong|Mao Zedong]]'s policies but grew after the reform and opening up, and Zhejiang is now one of China's wealthiest provinces, ranking fourth in GDP nationally, with a nominal GDP of US$1.27 trillion as of 2024. Hangzhou marks the end of the [[Grand Canal (China)|Grand Canal]] and includes the notable [[West Lake|West Lake]].

Chinese admiral and diplomat of the early [[Ming dynasty|Ming dynasty]]. Born a Muslim named Ma He in Yunnan, he was captured as a youth during the Ming conquest of the province, castrated, and placed in the household of Zhu Di, later the [[Yongle Emperor|Yongle Emperor]]. He assisted the future emperor in the Jingnan campaign that overthrew the Jianwen Emperor in 1402, and was given the surname Zheng. He rose to command the southern capital [[Nanjing|Nanjing]]. Between 1405 and 1433 he commanded seven treasure voyages across Asia for the Yongle Emperor and the succeeding Xuande Emperor. The expeditions brought a new militaristic presence to the [[Indian Ocean|Indian Ocean]] and extended state-controlled trade networks as far as the Swahili coast of Africa. According to legend, his largest ships were almost twice as long as any wooden ship ever recorded and carried hundreds of sailors on four decks. The Hongxi Emperor suspended further voyages after the Yongle Emperor's death in 1424.

Capital and largest city of [[Henan|Henan]] Province, China (pop., 2021: 12.6 million). Situated on the southern bank of the [[Yellow River|Yellow River]] where its valley widens into the [[North China Plain|North China Plain]], it is considered a cradle of Chinese civilization. An early [[Shang dynasty|Shang dynasty]] urban center was on the site, and the city later became the seat of a prefectural administration under the [[Sui dynasty|Sui dynasty]]. In June 1938, during the [[Second Sino-Japanese War|Second Sino-Japanese War]], Nationalist forces breached dikes at Huayuankou, north of the city, to hinder the Japanese advance; the Yellow River did not return to its original course until 1947. In the 1990s, following [[Reform and opening up|reform and opening up]], its gross domestic product grew from ¥2.03 billion in 1978 to over ¥100 billion by 2003. The Zhengzhou Commodity Exchange was the first futures exchange approved by the State Council, in October 1990. The city is home to the headquarters of Yutong Bus, the largest bus manufacturer in the world by sales volume.

Chinese Buddhist monk, philosopher and meditation teacher who founded the Tiantai tradition and is counted as its fourth patriarch. He built a comprehensive religious system on Chinese interpretations of [[Mahayana|Mahayana]] Buddhism, based mainly on the *Lotus Sutra*. His innovations included the Threefold Truth, which unifies the truths of emptiness and provisional existence with a holistic third truth, the middle. According to David W. Chappell, he has been ranked with [[Thomas Aquinas|Thomas Aquinas]] and [[Al-Ghazali|al-Ghazali]] as one of the great systematizers of religious thought and practice in world history. His *Mohe Zhiguan* outlines step-by-step instructions for [[Meditation|meditation]], combining traditional Indian methods with unique innovations, and it remains an influential guide across East Asian Buddhist traditions. His Tiantai school became one of the most significant Buddhist traditions in imperial China and spread to Korea and Japan, and his works influenced Chan/Zen, Pure Land and Nichiren Buddhism.

Chinese statesman and diplomat who was the first premier of the People's Republic of China from October 1949 until his death. One of the [[Chinese Communist Party|Chinese Communist Party]]'s earliest leaders, he was subordinate to [[Mao Zedong|Mao Zedong]] after the Zunyi Conference, but helped Mao consolidate power and shape foreign policy. As foreign minister from 1949 to 1958, he advocated peaceful coexistence with the West after the [[Korean War|Korean War]], attending the 1954 [[Geneva|Geneva]] Conference and the 1955 [[Bandung|Bandung]] Conference. He helped orchestrate [[Richard Nixon|Richard Nixon]]'s 1972 visit to China and steered relations with the United States and the [[Soviet Union|Soviet Union]]. As premier during the [[Cultural Revolution|Cultural Revolution]], he kept the government and economy functioning, remained deferential to Mao, and tried to shield some people from purges and persecution. After the fall of Lin Biao, he was elected first-ranking vice chairman of the party in 1973.

Royal dynasty of China that existed for 790 years, from c. 1046 BC until 256 BC, the longest span of any dynasty in Chinese history. During the Western Zhou period (c. 1046–771 BC), the royal house had military control over territories centered on the Wei River valley and North China Plain. Its suzerainty became increasingly ceremonial in the Eastern Zhou period (771–256 BC), which included the [[Spring and Autumn period|Spring and Autumn period]] and the [[Warring States period|Warring States period]], marked by large-scale warfare among former client states. The Zhou were formally extinguished by the state of Qin in 256 BC, and the [[Qin dynasty|Qin dynasty]] was founded in 221 BC after the conquest of all China. The Zhou era is considered the zenith of Chinese bronzeware. Its later period saw the advent of [[Confucianism|Confucianism]], [[Taoism|Taoism]] and [[Legalism (Chinese philosophy)|Legalism]]. The dynasty's legitimacy rested on the [[Mandate of Heaven|Mandate of Heaven]] doctrine.

Chinese philosopher, historian, politician and poet of the Southern [[Song dynasty|Song dynasty]], and a leading figure in the development of Neo-Confucianism. His commentaries and editions of the Four Books, including the [[Analects|Analects]] and [[Mencius|Mencius]], became the core texts of the imperial civil service examinations from 1313 until their abolition in 1905. He emphasized the "investigation of things" and meditation as essential to moral and intellectual self-cultivation, and he criticized Buddhist approaches that claimed insight detached from ritual and learning. His thought became the official state ideology of China from the [[Yuan dynasty|Yuan dynasty]] onward and was later adopted in Japan, Korea and Vietnam. He wrote, compiled or edited almost a hundred books, and his followers recorded thousands of his conversations.

Ancient Chinese text that is one of the two foundational texts of [[Taoism|Taoism]], alongside the *Tao Te Ching*. Written in the late [[Warring States period|Warring States]] period and named for its traditional author, Zhuang Zhou, it consists of stories, maxims, allegories, parables and fables, often irreverent or humorous. Its themes include spontaneity and freedom from human conventions, and it illustrates the arbitrariness of dichotomies such as good and bad, life and death, or human and nature. The only complete version has 33 chapters, prepared around AD 300 by Guo Xiang from an earlier form of 52. The first seven chapters are traditionally attributed to Zhuang Zhou himself, while the rest are generally considered later accretions. Regarded as one of the greatest works of [[Classical Chinese|Classical Chinese]] literature, it has influenced Chinese writers for more than two millennia.

Chinese statesman and strategist, the principal architect of the Shu Han state during the [[Three Kingdoms|Three Kingdoms]] period. After Liu Bei sought him out three times, Zhuge Liang proposed the Longzhong Plan and became Liu Bei's chief strategist. His role in the alliance that led to [[Cao Cao|Cao Cao]]'s defeat at the Battle of Red Cliffs was key. As chancellor and regent for the young Liu Shan, he held near-total authority over civil and military affairs. He governed with strict discipline, clear laws and meritocratic appointments, and his political thought blended [[Confucianism|Confucianism]] with [[Legalism (Chinese philosophy)|Legalism]]. He pacified the southwest and led repeated northern expeditions against Cao Wei. His *Chu Shi Biao*, an address of loyalty and statecraft to Liu Shan, is regarded as a masterpiece of Chinese prose. His legacy was immortalized in the 14th-century novel *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, which portrays him as a near-sage embodiment of wisdom and loyalty.

Stepped temple tower in the Sumerian city of [[Ur|Ur]], in present-day Dhi Qar Province, [[Iraq|Iraq]]. King Ur-Nammu of the Third Dynasty of Ur built it in the 21st century BC as a shrine to the moon god Nanna, the patron deity of Ur. The step pyramid measured 64 m (210 ft) long, 45 m (148 ft) wide and over 30 m (98 ft) high, although the height is speculative because only the foundations survived. The last Neo-Babylonian king, Nabonidus, restored it in seven stages rather than three in the 6th century BC. Excavations led by Sir Leonard Woolley in the 1920s and 1930s found a three-layered mass of mud brick faced with burnt brick set in bitumen. Under [[Saddam Hussein|Saddam Hussein]] in the 1980s, the façade and monumental staircase were partly reconstructed. The structure was damaged in the [[Gulf War|Gulf War]] in 1991, and its walls bear more than 400 bullet holes. It is the best-preserved ziggurat in [[Mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] apart from that of Dur Untash (Chogha Zanbil).

Landlocked country in southeastern Africa (pop., 2026: 17.3 million), with its capital at [[Harare|Harare]]. Bantu peoples settled the region about 2,000 years ago, and the Shona people built [[Great Zimbabwe|Great Zimbabwe]], a major trade center by the 13th century. The British South Africa Company of [[Cecil Rhodes|Cecil Rhodes]] conquered Mashonaland in 1890 and Matabeleland in 1893, and in 1923 the area became the self-governing colony of Southern Rhodesia. In 1965 the white minority government declared independence as [[Rhodesia|Rhodesia]]. A 15-year guerrilla war ended in a peace agreement that established Zimbabwe in April 1980. [[Robert Mugabe|Robert Mugabe]] became prime minister in 1980 and president from 1987; his authoritarian regime was responsible for widespread human rights violations. Economic decline from 1997 to 2008, including hyperinflation, was followed by growth after the use of other currencies was permitted. Mugabe resigned in 2017 following a coup, and Emmerson Mnangagwa has since served as president.

Chemical element with the symbol Zn and atomic number 30. A bluish-white [[Transition metal|transition metal]] and the first element in group 12 of the periodic table, zinc is the 24th most abundant element in Earth's crust, at an average concentration of 70 grams per ton. Its most common ore is sphalerite (zinc blende), and the largest economically feasible deposits are in China, Peru and Australia. [[Brass|Brass]], an alloy of copper and zinc, was used as early as the third millennium BC. Hot-dip galvanization, which coats iron with corrosion-resistant zinc, is its major application. Zinc is an essential trace element and the second most abundant trace metal in humans after [[Iron|iron]], a cofactor for many [[Enzyme|enzymes]]. Deficiency affects about two billion people in the developing world. Zinc sulfide is used in luminescent [[Paint|paints]], and zinc gluconate is used as a [[Dietary supplement|dietary supplement]].

French football manager and former attacking midfielder who has been head coach of the France national team since July 2026. Widely regarded as one of the greatest players of all time, he was known for his elegance, vision and ball control. He played for [[Bordeaux|Bordeaux]] and [[Juventus FC|Juventus]], winning two [[Serie A|Serie A]] titles, before moving to Real Madrid in 2001 for a world-record fee of €77.5 million. He scored a left-foot volley in the 2002 [[UEFA Champions League|UEFA Champions League]] final. Capped 108 times by France, he scored twice in the final of the 1998 [[FIFA World Cup|FIFA World Cup]] and was named Player of the Tournament at [[UEFA European Championship|UEFA Euro 2000]]. He won the 1998 Ballon d'Or and was named FIFA World Player of the Year three times. As a coach, he led Real Madrid to three consecutive Champions League titles and was the ambassador for [[Qatar|Qatar]]'s successful bid to host the 2022 World Cup.

Jewish nationalist movement that emerged in late 19th-century Europe to establish a Jewish homeland in [[Palestine (region)|Palestine]]. Responding to antisemitism and the Haskalah, it was led by [[Theodor Herzl|Theodor Herzl]] and was the main force behind the creation of the State of [[Israel|Israel]] in 1948. The 1917 [[Balfour Declaration|Balfour Declaration]] supported "the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people." Zionist views vary, including Liberal, Labor, Revisionist, Cultural and Religious Zionism. Supporters describe it as a national liberation movement, while critics often characterize it as supremacist, colonialist or racist.

Device for binding together the two edges of an opening in fabric or other flexible material. Its two rows of metal or plastic teeth are joined or separated by a slider with a Y-shaped channel, which makes the characteristic zip sound. Zippers appear in jackets, jeans, luggage, tents and sleeping bags, and they can enlarge or restrict an opening, join garment parts or decorate an item. American inventor Whitcomb L. Judson of Chicago patented an early design that proved unreliable. Elias Howe had patented a related fastening in 1851 but did not market it. The modern form owes much to the Swedish-born engineer Gideon Sundback, who introduced more closely spaced interlocking teeth. The name came from a brand of rubber galoshes on which the fastener was used in 1923, and hookless fasteners soon came to be called zippers.

Zirconium silicate mineral (ZrSiO₄) and the main source of [[Zirconium|zirconium]] metal. Hafnium is almost always present in quantities of 1 to 4%. Zircon occurs as an accessory mineral in [[Igneous rock|igneous]], [[Metamorphic rock|metamorphic]] and [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary]] rocks, and it is highly resistant to weathering. Colorless and transparent varieties are prized as [[Gemstone|gemstones]], and colorless zircon can resemble [[Diamond|diamond]] when cut. Because it incorporates uranium and thorium but excludes lead, zircon is used in uranium-lead dating. The oldest known zircon grains, from Western Australia's Jack Hills, date to about 4.4 billion years ago.

Chemical element with symbol Zr and atomic number 40, a lustrous [[Transition metal|transition metal]] that closely resembles [[Hafnium|hafnium]]. It was identified in 1789, isolated in impure form in 1824 and manufactured at scale by 1925. The name derives from the mineral [[Zircon|zircon]], its most important source. Ductile, malleable and corrosion-resistant, it is mostly produced as a byproduct of minerals mined for [[Titanium|titanium]] and [[Tin|tin]]. Zirconium is mainly used as a refractory and opacifier, and its alloys clad nuclear fuel rods because of their low neutron absorption and strong corrosion resistance. Other uses include flashbulbs, dental implants, deodorant and water purification systems. Its main hazards are flammability in powder form and irritation of the eyes.

Swedish former striker known for acrobatic strikes and volleys, regarded as one of the greatest strikers of all time. He won 34 trophies, including four consecutive [[Ligue 1|Ligue 1]] titles with Paris Saint-Germain, and scored more than 500 club goals. He also played for Ajax, Juventus, [[Inter Milan|Inter Milan]], [[AC Milan|AC Milan]] and Manchester United. His 35-yard bicycle kick for Sweden against England won the FIFA Puskás Award in 2013. He was Sweden's record goalscorer with 62 goals and scored in four consecutive decades, from the 1990s to the 2020s.

Unidentified serial killer who murdered at least five people in the [[San Francisco Bay Area|San Francisco Bay Area]] between December 1968 and October 1969. In letters sent to Bay Area newspapers, the killer claimed the murders and included cryptograms; two of the four were decrypted, in 1969 and 2020. The only suspect police named was Arthur Leigh Allen, a former elementary school teacher and convicted sex offender. The killer claimed 37 victims in a letter to the San Francisco Chronicle in 1974. The case remains unsolved, and the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|Federal Bureau of Investigation]] and several local agencies maintain it as open.

Belt-shaped region of the sky, about 8° north and south of the [[Ecliptic|ecliptic]], the apparent path of the [[Sun|Sun]] across the celestial sphere. It is divided into twelve signs of 30° each, which roughly correspond to [[Constellation|constellations]] from Aries through Pisces. The system originated in [[Babylonia|Babylonian]] astronomy during the 1st millennium BC and reached Greek astronomy by the 2nd century BC. Because of precession, the March equinox has moved from Aries into Pisces. The ecliptic coordinate system based on the zodiac is still used in astronomy for tracking Solar System objects. The names of the signs are mostly associated with horoscopic [[Astrology|astrology]], and the term may also refer to the East Asian twelve-year cycle known as the [[Chinese zodiac|Chinese zodiac]]. In the 2nd century AD, [[Ptolemy|Ptolemy]] described its construction in the *Almagest*.

Legendary undead being reanimated from a corpse, originally a figure of [[Haiti|Haitian]] folklore. In [[Haitian Vodou|Haitian Vodou]] belief, a bokor sorcerer reanimates a dead body by magic. Dictionaries trace the English word, first recorded in the 18th century, to Bantu languages such as Kimbundu. In the 20th century, Western fiction transformed the zombie into a contagious, cannibalistic undead person. This version was largely drawn from George A. Romero's *Night of the Living Dead* (1968), in which infection, disease or radiation often replaced magic as the cause. The zombie became a staple of video games such as [[Resident Evil|Resident Evil]] and of the "zombie apocalypse" concept seen in *The Walking Dead*. Since the late 2000s, zombies have also been portrayed sympathetically, as friends and love interests.
